Pele Yoetz 208:3: And it is right to pray for the welfare of one's fellow Israelite, and all the more so for the welfare of the sages, judges and officers, for were it not for the fear of them too, men would swallow each other alive. And it is known that the law of the kingdom is the law (Gittin 10b). Thus those who hide themselves and flee from the king's labor obligations do not do well, and certainly, all the more so, those who hide and smuggle to avoid customs duties, for they thereby commit robbery, also transgressing “and you shall greatly guard your souls” (Deuteronomy 4:15). Likewise those who secretly act against the laws of the kingdom, called contraband, place themselves in tremendous danger and rely on a miracle, and if a miracle is done for them, it is deducted from their merits. Therefore let one bear this until the Lord grants us rest from Heaven and breaks the yoke of the nations from off our neck, and restores our captivity as before — so may it be [His] will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 209:1: Mora (Reverence) — We were commanded several kinds of reverence. The first of these is what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:3), “Each man shall revere his mother and his father.” And I have seen that even distinguished people, and they are few, have reverence for father and mother only when they fear being struck with a rod on their head, drawing blood; but once they are somewhat grown, they cast it off and do not do even one part in a thousand of what they are obligated to do. Woe to the children from the Day of Judgment, for God will certainly bring everything into judgment. Whoever desires life should gird his loins like a man, and do whatever is in his power to do of what is incumbent upon him. And I have already written above that it is fitting for the father to forgo his honor toward his children in order to lighten their punishment, although in any case they cannot be entirely saved from punishment except through proper repentance, as is known — at least let this take away half. And I further say that if the Sages said (Yevamot 65b) that just as it is a commandment to say something that will be heeded, so it is a commandment not to say something that will not be heeded, how much more so should a father be careful not to burden and command his children with something he fears they will not obey, thereby transgressing “you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14), in the manner of what they said (Mo'ed Katan 17a) regarding one who strikes his grown son, and thereby causing pain above through his son's sin, and increasing the weight of the Divine Presence's wings in exile, as is known. Therefore let every prudent person act with understanding according to his son's understanding and disposition, weighing carefully and hitting the mark precisely, without erring.
Pele Yoetz 209:2: There is also the reverence due the Temple, in whose place we now have the synagogue, which is for us a small sanctuary. And it is already known that they were very strict in the holy Zohar (Parashat Terumah, p. 131) about the prohibition of speaking in the synagogue, to the point that they said that whoever converses in the synagogue diminishes his faith, etc., and has no share in the God of Israel. And I have already said that regarding such matters, the rabbis cry out and expound on them from time to time, yet no one takes it to heart to abandon their bad custom, but rather the world follows its usual way. To you, O men, I call: have regard for your Maker's honor and for your own souls, and take to heart to hear the words of the wise and to turn from evil and do good with all your heart, and you shall delight your soul in fatness. And if this is difficult for you, weigh the loss of the transgression, for the reward is according to the pain. Part of the reverence due the synagogue is not to speak there loudly as in the streets of the city, and even if one sees a person there committing a transgression and wishes to prevent the wrongdoing, he should not raise his voice loudly and greatly, but rather picture himself as standing before the King in the King's palace, and clothe himself in dread, for even a raised voice in the synagogue brings disgrace and wrath as it did upon Miriam, and God will bring everything into judgment, and the words of the wise are heard in gentleness (Ecclesiastes 9:17).
Pele Yoetz 209:3: There is also the reverence one must have for the sages, as our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Pesachim 22b) on “you shall revere the Lord your God” — to include Torah scholars. This shows that their reverence was equated with the reverence of Heaven. And through our sins, many unlearned people greatly belittle the honor of Torah scholars and disgrace them, and woe to them, for in the end they will be burned by their own coal, whether in this world or in the World to Come. And it is true that the masses should not be blamed so much for this, since they do not know the severity of the prohibition, because the Torah scholars refrain from expounding on this matter lest people say they expound it for their own honor. But in any case, they already hear in the synagogue from schoolchildren who read Pirkei Avot, where it is said (Avot 2:10), “Warm yourself before the fire of the sages, but be careful of their coals lest you be burned.” And even though we do not now have the [full legal] status of Torah scholars, the commentators have already written that just as Torah scholars have diminished in stature, so too the masses have descended tremendously in stature from that of earlier generations, and Yiftach in his generation is like Samuel in his generation (Rosh Hashanah 25b).
Pele Yoetz 210:1: Menuchah (Rest) — Rest, for it is good, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 114a), “Eat an onion and sit in the shade.” And it is already told (see Chovot HaLevavot, Gate of Trust, introduction to the tenth discussion) of a certain pious man who used to pray, God save us, from “dispersion of the soul,” meaning dispersion of money, which is dispersion of the soul. And they said (Proverbs 17:1), “Better a dry morsel with quiet than [a house full of feasting] with strife.” And they said (Kiddushin 82b), “A man should always teach his son a clean and easy trade and pray to the One to whom wealth belongs.” And one who believes in the Lord and trusts in Him truly and with complete faith, that He gives strength to do valiantly and that there is no restraint upon the Lord to save, whether by much or by little; and if one runs like a deer and toils to become rich and labors greatly, the one who does much will not exceed what has been allotted him from Heaven, and the one who does little will not lack — such a person will choose rest, for it is good, for the service of the blessed Name, and will not go on the roads that exhaust his strength and shorten his days, as it is written (Psalms 102:24), “He weakened my strength on the way; He shortened my days.” And all roads are presumed dangerous, and if a miracle is done for him, it is deducted from his merits, and woe to a person who loses merits in order to gain money. And how many mishaps befall travelers on the road, and above all is the great loss of forgoing the service of God and communal prayer while on the road, and it will not succeed. And people already say, “Where there is no blessing [recited over the meal, i.e., proper settlement], there is no blessing.” And truly they said, “Happy are those who dwell in Your house.”
Pele Yoetz 210:2: Likewise, one who trusts in the Lord and believes in Him with complete faith should choose a clean and easy trade and a business arrangement that does not involve so much trouble and dispersion of the soul, and certainly should not lose much good by failing to pray with the congregation morning, afternoon, and evening, and should not commit injustice, God forbid, and should not say that whoever does not do so [i.e., engage in strenuous business] does not eat bread in this age, for whoever says this speaks falsely, for man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord (Deuteronomy 8:3), and there is no restraint upon the Lord to save. On the contrary, one who trusts in the Lord and does good will be satisfied with bread and it will be well. And it is true that all depends on a person's deeds — sometimes it is decreed for him that his sustenance will come through labor and toil and that he will have dispersion of the soul. And a person does not so much as bruise his finger below unless it is decreed from above (Chullin 7b), but truly they said (Makkot 10b), “In the way a person wishes to go, he is led.” And it is a person's duty to strive with great strength and vigor, and to make do with little, in order to seek quiet, settlement, and rest, for it is good for the service of the blessed Name, and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 210:3: And the essential rest that a person should seek for himself is the rest of the World to Come; therefore let him incline his shoulder and bear the burden, and not wither. Let him not be disgusted by rebuke, and let him weigh the reward of a commandment against its loss (Avot, beginning of ch. 2), for better is one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world (ibid. 4:17).
Pele Yoetz 211:1: Mitzvot (Commandments) — Happy is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in His commandments (Psalms 112:1). And a man who is a Jew and believes in the Lord, who gives good reward to those who keep His commandments and a bad and bitter punishment to those who transgress His commandments, it is fitting for him to run after a commandment and toil after it to attain it with all his strength, all his soul and all his might, even more than one who toils to earn a thousand thousand gold coins, and even more than one who runs after life [itself], for the reward given for commandments is very great.
Pele Yoetz 211:2: Go and learn that for the sake of two acts of running that Abraham our father performed — as it is written, “and he ran to meet them” (Genesis 18:2), and “and Abraham ran to the cattle” (ibid., v. 7) — for this alone the Holy One, blessed be He, cannot move away from Israel, as it is written (Song of Songs 7:6), “A king is held captive in the tresses,” as our sages, of blessed memory, said in the midrash (Song of Songs Rabbah 7). And for the commandment of honoring one's father that Esau the wicked performed, he and his descendants merited [reward] until the coming of our Messiah (Devarim Rabbah 17), and likewise Ishmael for the sake of circumcision (Yalkut, Parashat Toldot, remez 14). And likewise Nebuchadnezzar the wicked, for the four steps he took in honor of the Omnipresent, merited the great honor of ruling as though holding the world in his palm, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 96a), and many such cases. And all this is vanity and emptiness compared to the reward given for commandments in the future to come, which is a delight that a person cannot understand or estimate while in this world, to the point that they said (Avot 4:17), “Better is one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world,” even if one were king over the whole earth.
Pele Yoetz 211:3: On the other hand, the punishment for transgressions and neglect of commandments is severe, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward for any commandment, even for pleasant conversation or a good thought (Bava Kamma 38b; Nazir 23b), nor does He forgo any transgression or neglect of a commandment, even the smallest of the small, for God will bring everything into judgment. And woe to people from the Day of Judgment and the Day of Reckoning, for one will be held accountable even for transgressions that people trample underfoot, which have become as though permitted, and for neglect of grave commandments and of light ones even more than of grave ones, and woe to people for the disgrace shown to commandments (see Avot ch. 1), which they do not value even as much as the profit of a single zuz. And if you ask anyone called by the name of Israel, “Tell me, how much is a single commandment worth?” he will answer, “All treasures cannot equal it.” And everyone in the world knows and believes that the Holy One, blessed be He, gives good reward to the righteous and a bad and bitter punishment to the wicked, and they say so with their mouths in the declaration recited every eve of Rosh Chodesh, but their deeds are the opposite, for they do not guard against transgression even as much as a person guards against losing a single zuz, and they neglect a commandment even for the benefit of a single zuz, and do not pursue it as a person pursues earning a single zuz, and sometimes they neglect several commandments, such as praying morning, afternoon, and evening with the congregation, and congregational responses, and acts of kindness, and many others, and neglect of Torah study outweighs all of them, even without any benefit at all.
Pele Yoetz 211:4: Thus they transgress several transgressions for no benefit at all, but simply from not taking to heart the fear and love of the honored and awesome Lord, the dreadful and awesome King, and from not understanding that for every commandment he could fulfill and does not fulfill, and for every transgression he commits, it shows that he has no regard for his Maker's honor, of whom our sages, of blessed memory, said that it would have been better for him not to have come into the world (Chagigah 11b), since he does not care to give delight to his Maker, and is not concerned about causing pain and anger to the exalted and uplifted King, and blemishing all the worlds and delaying the Messiah's coming, and many such evils that several books could not fully describe.
Pele Yoetz 211:5: And if a person says, “Who does not know all this, that better is one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17), and that it is evil and bitter to forsake the Lord and transgress His commandments more than any evil in the world, and we know which is the straight path” — but we have a strong argument, that the inclination of man's heart is evil and hard as iron. To this too I say that the whole world knows that this argument does not exempt them from the great and awesome Day of Judgment, for the Holy One, blessed be He, has already said (Kiddushin 30b), “I have created the evil inclination, I have created for it the Torah as a remedy,” for the light within it brings them back to good, and even if it [the heart] is iron, it shatters. And the Holy One, blessed be He, created the evil inclination for man's benefit, so that he subdue it and receive reward, for the reward is according to the pain. And if a person says [as they said] (Berachot 5b), “Neither they nor their reward,” [meaning, why does he need this trial at all,] why does he need life — for before his coming into the world he was sustained by charity like the ministering angels, and the Holy One, blessed be He, did not send him into this world except so that he benefit from his own labor by subduing his inclination, and he should rejoice upon seeing his inclination entice him with a double enticement to commit a transgression or neglect a commandment, for then he can rise up like a lion to subdue his inclination, knowing with certainty that the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to give him merit and increase his reward, for they said (Avot DeRabbi Natan, ch. 3, near end) that reward is given for a commandment performed, or a transgression from which one withdraws his hand while his inclination overpowers him, more than for a hundred commandments performed when his inclination does not overpower him. And no person can say, “I was unable to stand guard against a certain transgression,” or “I could not muster the strength to fulfill a certain commandment,” for whatever a man desires to do, he can do, and he can bring his deeds to the level of the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the righteous, for they too were born of woman and had an evil inclination just as we do. And even now, in every single generation there are righteous men.
Pele Yoetz 211:6: And the man who desires life should not follow the majority for evil, and his heart should not envy sinners, but rather be in fear of the Lord all day. And let not the young men say, “This is a time for play and merriment and joy and to pursue every desire, for youth comes but once and will not return, and days will come when there will be a desire to fulfill every commandment, once the days of old age arrive” — for this is vanity and vexation of spirit for several reasons. First, a person does not know his time nor what a day may bring, for perhaps tomorrow he will come and be no more, for death does not delay, and especially in this time death is common, God have mercy. Furthermore, one who says, “I will sin and then repent,” is not given the opportunity to repent (Yoma 85b). And also, once he grows old, he will not turn from his evil way. Furthermore, God will bring into judgment even the days of youth, for all that has passed, and for all the commandments neglected and the great pursuit of desires, and the service and judgment will weigh more heavily upon young men, for while they had the power — as a man in his vigor — to do good and fulfill every commandment and walk in the ways of repentance, they spent their strength and their days on vanity and emptiness by pursuing every desire. Therefore, O people of the Lord, servants of the Lord, small with great, elders with youths, let us be strong and strengthen ourselves and have regard for our Maker's honor, and also have regard for our own souls, and flee from every transgression and pursue every commandment and every good trait, with all our heart and all our soul and all our might, and the Lord God will help us, for one who comes to purify himself is helped from Heaven (Shabbat 104b).
Pele Yoetz 211:7: And one must be especially diligent to fulfill every commandment that involves financial loss, and to be careful of every transgression in a place involving financial loss, for the nearby inclination grows strong over a person, especially in these generations, a generation of money, where a person is recognized by his pocket, so that money should not be considered anything in his eyes when weighed against a hint of transgression, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent even for one hour. And one who loves the Lord as is fitting should give all the wealth of his house out of love, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:5), “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your might [me'odecha, also meaning wealth].” This is a shrewd man, a sharp merchant, comparable to one who buys a pearl beyond price for the value of a mere perutah — so too, for the price of despised money he has acquired for himself words of Torah, acquired for himself life in the World to Come, and moreover, even in this world he enjoys the fruits and has abundant silver, wealth and riches in his house (Psalms 112:3), and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing. And there are several conditions required for fulfilling commandments so that they be accepted with favor, and they are written in Sefer Chareidim and Sefer Lev David — go and see.
Pele Yoetz 212:1: Mezakeh (One Who Brings Merit) — The saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Avot 5:18): whoever brings merit to the many, the merit of the many is suspended upon him. And greater than this they said (ibid., v. 19): whoever brings merit to the many, no sin comes about through him. There are several kinds of bringing merit. One is through Torah, such as teaching the people knowledge and the fear of the Lord, and which is the straight path, and constantly expounding to the public words of ethics and God's statutes and His teachings — perhaps on some day his words will bear fruit, if not for a hundred out of a thousand, or for ten, then at least for one. And how good and pleasant it is to write in a book summaries of laws and words of ethics and upright conduct, and in the vernacular for those who speak other languages, for this is like expounding before tens of thousands of Israel, and perhaps in some generation, for some Israelite man, his words will bear fruit and he will bring him merit. And it is known how greatly they extolled in the holy Zohar (Shemot, p. 128) the essential reward and the great honor bestowed upon one who brings merit to another — wonder of wonders.
Pele Yoetz 212:2: Thus, let a person be firm in strengthening himself, and with the spirit of his lips rebuke others. And this is a commandment upon every person, not the wise alone — rather, “let each man help his fellow, and say to his brother, be strong” (Isaiah 41:6), and let us strengthen one another to give delight to our Creator. Included in bringing merit is reciting blessings aloud so that people may answer “Amen,” especially the blessings recited by those called to the Torah, for some say that if he did not make his voice heard so that the congregation could answer “Amen,” his blessings are in vain, for these blessings are recited by the one called up on behalf of the entire congregation, and he fulfills the obligation of the many (Orach Chaim, sec. 139, para. 6). And it is known that great is the one who answers “Amen” (Berachot 53b), and according to the greatness of the commandment, so is the reward of the one who brings merit.
Pele Yoetz 212:3: Likewise it is included in bringing merit that when standing among a gathering of people, or at meals, one should open his mouth with words of Torah, and even one who does not know any words of Torah should ask a Torah scholar among them even something simple in words of Torah, and by opening a door to it, Torah will flow and spread, and one thereby causes the fulfillment of what the Sages said (Avot 3:4): three who eat at one table and speak words of Torah over it, etc., and that they not transgress the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (ibid., v. 3) that two who sit together without words of Torah between them, etc. Likewise it is included in bringing merit to strive to establish ordinances and upright practices in one's city, such as providing food for the poor at the entrance of the synagogue and the like. In sum, whatever one can say, “Please, my brothers, do not do wrong,” and whatever can cause others to be brought to a commandment through his words, or through him others see and do likewise — the merit of the many depends on him.
Pele Yoetz 213:1: Mutarot (Excesses) — The evil of excess is known to be great, whether in food and drink, which destroys both soul and body — for if one eats and drinks excessively, his head and limbs become heavy upon him, and he can bring upon himself many illnesses. Likewise, if one crawls after fine foods and human pleasures, and after fine clothing and pleasant, airy, decorated and painted dwellings and upper chambers, he transgresses “do not destroy,” and all the more so if he spends beyond his means and the blessing the Lord has given him, causing harm to himself and possibly coming to borrow and not repay, or to rob and plunder, God forbid. And even if the Lord has graced him with wealth, it is fitting to be sparing with his money, for the Torah has regard for the money of Israel (Rosh Hashanah 27a), and the righteous hold their money dear more than their bodies, since they do not stretch out their hands in robbery (Chullin 91a), for when a person accustoms himself to living in luxury and wonders, if evil days come upon him, God forbid — for the wheel turns in the world — he will be forced to commit injustice and every evil vice in order to maintain his accustomed standard, as they said regarding the wayward and rebellious son (Sanhedrin 72a). But one who accustoms himself to the trait of contentment and makes do with little, all his days are good; and as for that excess which he spends in vain and which goes to waste, if he had given it to charity, how good his portion and how good his exchange would be. And even if one gives and does abundant charity and good deeds, this is still not a permission for him to throw his money away in waste, for the poor have not yet all been made wealthy.
Pele Yoetz 213:2: And another point regarding eating: our sages, of blessed memory, said that whatever a person eats on weekdays beyond what he needs to be healthy for the service of the blessed Name adds strength to the Sitra Achra and to the evil inclination to cause him to sin, and wastes precious time to earn more, and other time to eat more, and yet other time to spend more. And how much effort is needed to earn, and effort to prepare, and effort to expel from the body — and all the pleasures and delights of this world are vanity and vexation of spirit, utter vanity with no substance, the deceptions of the evil inclination and blindness of the eyes.
Pele Yoetz 213:3: Whoever desires life should be firm in strengthening himself against his inclination, and make do with less food and drink than he actually has; and likewise regarding clothing and dwellings, let him choose a middle path in accordance with the blessing the Lord has given him, and not pursue excess, but rather give the excess to charity for the toilers of Torah and thereby acquire for himself life in the World to Come. And so we find with David, king of Israel, who said (I Chronicles 22:14), “And behold, in my affliction I have prepared,” which our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:1) to mean that by limiting his own enjoyment and royal pleasures, he set aside funds for building the Temple and gathered great wealth. We too have learned (Avot 1:5), “Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household.” And the commentators explained that in order to be able to keep your house open wide, you must accustom the members of your household to make do with little, like the poor, and if you do so, happy are you and it is well with you.
Pele Yoetz 214:1: Mehirut – Matun (Haste and Deliberation) — Haste has a side that is not good, as I wrote above under the entry Hachanah [Preparation]. But there is also a side on which haste is very good, as it is said (Proverbs 22:29), “Do you see a man diligent in his work? He shall stand before kings.” This means that once a person has decided in his mind that he should do a certain thing, whether in mundane matters or matters of Heaven, he should hasten to do it quickly. In mundane matters, so that he not be preoccupied and his heart turn to the service of the blessed Name; and in matters of Heaven, he should leap and perform the commandment, for it is better to do it one hour earlier, and he should not let a commandment that comes his way go stale, for he does not know what a day may bring, and how many hindrances, distractions and enticements of the evil inclination can arise from moment to moment. Whoever is diligent is rewarded, and this too is included in “do His will as your own will” — for just as it is His will that people hasten to do His command, and if His servant delays, He fixes His eyes on him and rebukes him, so too, to distinguish, a person should reckon with himself and fulfill the commandments of God, may His Name be blessed.
Pele Yoetz 214:2: But at first one must be deliberate and reflect, in mundane matters, whether it is right to do the thing or better to refrain. And even in matters of a commandment one must be deliberate to consider whether it is fitting to do it, so that it not become a commandment fulfilled through transgression, and so that he not come to regret what he did before. And once he has decided to do it, he should consider in what manner it is fitting to do it perfectly, as I have already written above under the entry Hachanah. And especially regarding legal judgment, the saying of the Tanna is known (Avot 1:1): “Be deliberate in judgment.” Whether in monetary matters or in matters of prohibition and permission, great deliberation is needed, for they are like mountains hanging by a hair. And whoever does not set his mind to its strength, it has felled many victims — permitting the forbidden and forbidding the permitted, and bearing the sin of robbery and false oaths; and of him our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:7), “Whoever is arrogant in rendering rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit,” and is called hated, detestable, unjust, accursed and abominable, and other such evils. Therefore those who sit on seats of judgment should clothe themselves in dread, and should not be ashamed to tell those asking or litigants, “Wait,” even in a case that seems to him already familiar — even so, let him go over it again and study it thoroughly, and not say anything until it is as clear to him as his own sister [is forbidden to him].
Pele Yoetz 214:3: Likewise, when he comes to render judgment and sentence upon the wicked, great deliberation is required — whether to render judgment to break the teeth of the wicked and root out evil, and sometimes it is proper to be strict in judgment so that all the people hear and fear; but one must weigh in the scales and balances of justice whether, God forbid, in the place of judgment the wicked man's presence there and the departure of the sword of the town [reputation] might cause them to go astray and add transgression to their sin, and the like. Above all, one must consider what is best — whether to act or to refrain, and in what manner it is proper to act. And whoever sits in judgment should pour out his soul before the Lord, great in counsel and mighty in deed, and may the Merciful One have mercy on him and guide him with good counsel from before Him, so that no mishap or anything uncorrected come from his hand, and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence. And more will be written on this in its place, under the entry Judgment and Law, God willing.
Pele Yoetz 215:1: Ma'aser (Tithe) — The virtue of tithing is known to be great, to the point that they said (Ta'anit 9a) that in every matter it is forbidden to test the Lord, except regarding tithes, as it is said (Malachi 3:10), “Bring the full tithe into the storehouse... and test Me now in this, says the Lord of Hosts, if I do not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing until there is no room enough to receive it, until your lips grow weary of saying enough.” And greater than this, they said in Midrash Rabbah (Shemot, ch. 41) on the verse “Righteousness is Yours, O Lord, and shame of face belongs to us” (Daniel 9:7): Rabbi Nechemiah said, even at the time we perform charity, we look at our own deeds and feel shame; the only time we come with boldness before Him is when we bring forth our tithes, as it is written (Deuteronomy 26:15), “Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven.” Up to here [the midrash]. This is a wondrous matter. And from the reward we may learn how much delight this gives to our Creator, that He gives such good reward; therefore it is fitting to strengthen oneself to fulfill this for the sake of Heaven, to give delight to our Creator, and honor will follow in the end. Happy is Israel; some scatter more than a tenth in commandment-related expenses, but it appears that the virtue of the tithe is to spend it according to a proper accounting, and one commandment leads to another, for by setting aside the tithe year after year and placing it in a separate purse, it becomes easier in his eyes to spend on commandments generously.
Pele Yoetz 215:2: And come and see the blindness of the eyes that the evil inclination causes us: a person lends money with interest in order to profit, especially in a secure place, though in truth there is no security in a human being who himself has no salvation, for God is the judge — He brings down one and raises up another. Even if he has come into great means, when he wishes to glance at it, it is gone, as is known, and no man would lend to the Lord with interest, although everyone knows this is secure — certain, without any doubt — for God is not a man that He should lie. But in spending on other commandments, the evil inclination has room to entice, since [it argues] there is no reward for commandments in this world, even though one does enjoy fruits here too, and “all is from Tishrei to Tishrei except for TaShRe”’ [Torah, Shabbat, Rosh Chodesh, Yom Tov, whose reward is only in the World to Come], and if one adds, they add to him, as known from the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Beitzah 16a; Vayikra Rabbah 30:1). But our evil inclination has overpowered us so greatly that it entices us not to set aside the tithe at all, even though the reward is right before our eyes, through charity, “wealth and riches in his house.” And even though he gives about the amount of a tithe anyway, this is nothing but laziness in bringing it to an accounting. And this is the delay of the evil inclination, so that he not give delight to his Creator and thereby lose much good.
Pele Yoetz 215:3: And there is one who, upon hearing these words — what this commandment is and what its reward is — his soul desires to fulfill it, but his difficulty is in setting aside from the principal first. And if the Lord has graced him with wealth, he must set aside a large amount all at once, and a person's eye is stingy, and thereby he holds himself back. And whoever weighs the reward of a commandment against its loss will not retreat before anything. In any case, I say that if one cannot subdue his inclination to set aside from the principal, he should not refrain from setting it aside, from the day he resolves to do so, from everything he earns from then on, and everything that comes into his hand — even a found object, or charity, or a gift, money or its equivalent. And if he does not fulfill this completely, at least he does something, and it helps to bring blessing to his house and to all his undertakings. And for one who is in pressing circumstances, the halachic authorities have already written that he has authorities to rely on for spending tithe money on food for his children who are older than six (see Yoreh De'ah 251 and the later authorities, and Pitchei Teshuvah 249:2), only that a careful accounting should be kept.
Pele Yoetz 215:4: And whoever wishes to fulfill this and the like should seek guidance from a book, or from the mouths of scholars, as to what is proper to do, and do accordingly; then he will succeed in his ways and act wisely. And it would be well in this and similar matters to conduct oneself thus: when one begins to act and walk in the way of the good, he should clarify that his resolutions are without a vow and without a formal acceptance, and yet, whatever comes from his mouth he should do, and not retreat even if the matter is difficult for him, and it will be as pleasing to the Lord as a fire-offering, and the Lord will command the blessing to be with him in all that he does.
Pele Yoetz 216:1: Musar (Ethical Instruction) — The virtue of studying ethical works is well known and famous, to the point that the commentators explained (Birkei Yosef, Orach Chaim, sec. 1, see there) that the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 30b), “I have created the evil inclination, I have created for it the Torah as a remedy,” and they said (ibid.), “draw it to the study hall; if it is stone, it will melt; if it is iron, it will shatter” — all this refers to the study of ethical works. And regarding the rabbi who does not persist in studying ethics, he has not tasted the taste of the fear of sin, and his way seems right in his own eyes, and his heart believes he is a proper Jew; and even if he hears or studies once in a jubilee, or hears words of ethics, it does not affect him and does not arouse him at all, and “the flesh of the dead does not feel the scalpel,” for their hearts have become as fat as suet because of their sins, which act as curtains that separate and dull the heart. And of this they said (Berachot 18b) that the wicked, in their lifetime, are called dead, for they are like the dead who do not feel the fear of the Lord and His love in the flames of the divine fire as they properly should, and thereby they do not rejoice at commandments more than one who finds abundant spoil, nor do they feel pain over transgressions more than one before whom his dead lies unburied, as would be proper. And all this depends on the purity of the soul.
Pele Yoetz 216:2: And behold, the ladder set up to ascend the mountain of the Lord and to acquire purity of soul is diligence in studying or hearing ethical books, for then one learns to fear the Lord. And as a man reads ethical books, he will find his own skirts full of sins and transgressions piled high, for what he thought was not a sin that he committed, he will find written in the book to be a great sin, a criminal sin — such as the prohibition of robbery and fraud, causing pain to one's fellow, false and vain oaths, mockery, flattery, lies, and hurried blessings that are void, benefiting without a blessing, and idle words, of which it is said (Malachi 2:17), “You have wearied the Lord with your words,” and slander, which is as grave as idolatry, illicit relations and bloodshed, and pride and anger and gazing at women, and many other evils, with the neglect of Torah study outweighing them all — all of which are very grave transgressions that many have trampled upon until they have become as though fully permitted, and no one takes it to heart to regret his evil and abandon his way. Indeed, when one persists in reading or hearing words of ethics day after day, “my speech shall drip as the rain” took hold — just as rain wears away stone, so words of ethics eventually pierce the heart of stone. He will go, step by step, in the way of the good, and his heart will understand and return and be healed. And it is known that all beginnings are hard, and it will seem difficult to him to study or hear words of ethics, and the words will not enter his ears, he will feel nothing — but in the end his heart will be humbled, and it will become sweet and pleasant to him. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Berachot 40a): “If you listen when old [i.e., established knowledge], you will listen when new; but if your heart turns away, you will no longer listen.” Therefore hold fast to ethical study, do not let go, and if you have grown lax, return to it. Be strong and let your heart take courage.
Pele Yoetz 216:3: And it is fitting to study all ethical books one after another, again and again, as a fixed law not to be transgressed, day by day and night by night. And even when reviewing books he has already read, they should seem new in his eyes, and he will find new arousal according to the time and the state of his soul, for not all times are equal, as a righteous man will find. And since they said that words coming from the heart enter the heart, how good it is to study Pirkei Avot and the ethical teachings of the Talmud and the Midrashim, and the holy book Reishit Chokhmah, and the book of the pious Rabbi Shelah, and all such holy books, all of them holy (and if God is with me, I shall gather sayings of ethical instruction, in brief, from all the holy books, matters that pierce the heart, each word fitly spoken, and for those who speak other languages, in the vernacular — may the Lord finish [this work] on my behalf and help me for the sake of the honor of His Name). And those who speak other languages should seek and pursue vernacular books, such as Tikkun HaNefesh, Shevet Musar, and the like, as one pursues a partridge in the mountains, or seeks to hear teachings.
Pele Yoetz 216:4: And even one whom the Lord has graced with knowledge and who has placed his portion among those who sit in the study hall, engaged in the laws of leprosy and tent-impurity, needs even more to study ethical books, for study is not the essential thing but rather practice (Avot 1:17), and whoever is greater than his fellow has a greater inclination against him (Sukkah 52a), and their unwitting errors are treated as deliberate sins, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with them to a hairsbreadth. And let no one say, “What need have I to study or hear teachings — everything is revealed and known to me of what is written in the books that speak of how one should serve and fear and love the honored and awesome Lord?” This is the counsel of the evil inclination, for the special virtue of studying ethical books is to arouse the heart, for a person applies his spirit to what he studies and wishes to be aroused, and studies in order to fulfill, keep and do — certainly these things bear fruit, and a right spirit is renewed within him.
Pele Yoetz 217:1: Machshavah (Thought) — A good thought, how great is its benefit, for all service depends upon it, as I wrote above under the entry Good Heart. And it is stated in the holy Zohar (part 1, p. 125) that according to what a person thinks, he draws upon himself — if matters of holiness, he draws holiness upon himself; if evil musings, he draws impurity upon himself and defiles his soul, and to the place he thinks of, there is his portion allotted. Thus it is fitting for a person to be firm in strengthening himself with great vigor to think pure thoughts, matters that bring a person to fear and love the honored and awesome Lord and to cling to Him, and to hold fast to humility, lowliness and other good and upright traits, and to reflect on the exaltedness of the blessed Name, for He is high above the highest and His greatness is beyond measure. Thus should he act constantly, to fulfill what the Torah said (Deuteronomy 6:5), “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” — meaning that his heart should not turn to share the love of other things with the love of the Lord, but rather all his love should be for the Lord, in such a way that all his love is according to the Torah, and all his deeds are for the sake of Heaven. And it is written (ibid., v. 6), “And these words shall be upon your heart,” etc., “when you sit in your house and when you walk on the way,” etc. And the plain sense of the verse implies that it means for the love of the Lord to be a constant remembrance. Likewise it is written (Leviticus 19:4), “Do not turn to the idols [elilim].” And our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Shabbat 149a), “Do not turn away from your own understanding [al da'atchem].” And there we have learned (Avot 3:4), “Whoever turns his heart to idleness endangers his own soul.” And truly it is great foolishness that, while a person is able to think pure thoughts of fear and love and the like, which are Torah commandments for which he receives reward, he instead turns his heart to idleness or entertains evil musings, for which he will be punished. Of this it is said (Jeremiah 2:13), “They have forsaken Me, the source of living waters, to hew for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns.”
Pele Yoetz 217:2: And it is true that the inclination of man's heart is evil, and a person has no control over his spirit, but nevertheless there is an obligation to strengthen oneself to replace evil and strange thoughts with pure thoughts, and to incite the good inclination against the evil inclination even a thousand times a day, and he will receive good reward for his labor, for he is helped from Heaven. And each time he remembers that he is not doing good by turning his heart to idleness or to evil musings, let him picture himself as one sinking in the mire of the deep, striving to get out, his heart crying out to his Father, “Save me, my Lord the King, deliver me from the mire.” And it is found written in the books of the Kabbalists that it is good, in order to nullify evil musings, to intend or mention the Name “Kera Satan” with its proper vocalization, and to recite the verse (Leviticus 6:6), “A perpetual fire shall be kept burning on the altar; it shall not go out,” and the verse (Psalms 119:113), “I hate those of a divided mind, but I love Your Torah,” and to pass his right hand over his forehead three times, and it will help with God's blessed assistance, provided he strives to divert his thought from the musings. And it is good to constantly intend the Name “Tarniel,” whose numerical value is [also that of] “Matzpetz,” to subdue the inclination which totals three hundred [in gematria].
Pele Yoetz 217:3: And our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Yoma 29a) that improper thoughts of sin are harder than the sin itself. And they also said (Bava Batra 164b) that no person is saved from improper thoughts of sin every day. However, the holy Rabbi, author of Reishit Chokhmah, wrote that if one does not dwell on his musing and flees from it at once, he will not be punished, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures; but if he dwells on his musing, he will surely be punished, for he causes himself harm, coming to a seminal emission and spilling seed in vain, which is graver than bloodshed. And they were very strict in the holy Zohar (Bereishit, p. 219) about this sin, to the point that one has almost no repentance for it and no share in the World to Come. It makes a person's hair stand on end to see its severity. Go and see in the holy book Reishit Chokhmah, chapter 17 of the Gate of Holiness, and in Seder HaYom and other holy books, and let there be a dread greater even than the dread of death.
Pele Yoetz 217:4: Thus, given the severity involved, it is fitting for a person to build a fence for a fence and a safeguard for a safeguard, in order to stand guard against improper thoughts and musings, and the great fence is to shut one's eyes from seeing evil (Isaiah 33:15), which our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Bava Batra 57a) to mean not gazing at forbidden women, for the eye and the heart are the two agents of sin — the eye sees and the heart devises thoughts of iniquity. And it is written (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray.” And besides the prohibition of gazing at forbidden women, which is itself a transgression — and we shall discuss this further below under the entry Sight, God willing — there is more: that one transgression drags another, so that even if one escapes the actual transgression, he does not escape improper thought, and he will surely be punished for arousing the evil inclination within her, in the manner of what they said (Niddah 13b), “One who deliberately induces his own emission should be under a ban,” because he arouses the evil inclination within him. And included in this is that one must be careful about what our sages, of blessed memory, warned us: not to hold the member even to urinate. And they said (ibid.) that whoever holds the member and urinates is as though he brings a flood upon the world. And there are distinctions in this matter between one married and one unmarried, and between above the corona and below it, as is explained in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim, sec. 3, para. 14) — see there.
Pele Yoetz 217:5: But given the severity involved, it is fitting to be strict in every way and to forbid it upon oneself entirely, not holding the member at all, but rather steadying himself by the scrotum or holding it through a garment. And this is a great principle for escaping every sin: to flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter even one gate of the forbidden, and certainly regarding so grave a prohibition as this, of which they said in the holy Zohar (Shemot, p. 26) that it is said of it (Job 19:29), “Be afraid of the sword for yourselves,” etc.
Pele Yoetz 217:6: And the great fence to escape evil musings is to marry in one's youth and to marry off his children close to their maturity, for they said (Kiddushin 29b) that once a man passes twenty years without marrying, all his days are spent in improper thoughts of sin. And certainly our holy sages are true and their words are true, and this is a great evil beyond compare. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to marry in his youth and to marry off his children close to their maturity, and not retreat before anything. Included in this is that he should not travel far on journeys so as to be without his wife for extended periods, for it is impossible to escape improper thoughts of sin and the transgression itself. And woe to those many evils found among men who travel far from their homes and dwell in the lands of Edom, full of those breached in forbidden relations, with no one to protest against them, and the marketplaces full of forgotten harlots who arouse the evil inclination like the venom of a serpent, and thus many have stumbled and fallen into the sin of seminal emission. And the man who is pure and God-fearing, though he escapes the actual transgression, does not escape improper thought, and will not remain pure of nocturnal emission. Woe to us, for this matter causes and delays the Messiah's coming.
Pele Yoetz 217:7: Therefore, whoever desires life, if he must trade in the lands of Edom for a long time, should acquire a partner, such that one of them remains in his own city while the other establishes his residence wherever it is his will to go, together with his wife with him. And if he does this, happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come, for it is not good for a person to be alone, neither for this world nor for the World to Come. And even if this increases his expenses, let him not worry, for all that a man has he will give for his life, and better a handful of quietness than two handfuls of labor and vexation of spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:6).
Pele Yoetz 217:8: And there is already a ban from our teacher Rabbeinu Gershom against remaining eighteen months away from home, brought in Be'er HaGolah, Yoreh De'ah, sec. 334 — see there. And no one heeds it, and I do not know the reason; and it does not succeed, for one who dwells without a wife dwells without blessing (Yevamot 62b), and although this is said of one who is unmarried, this too is included.
Pele Yoetz 217:9: And if it happens, God forbid, that some illness befalls a woman such that she cannot become ritually pure for her husband for an extended period, and likewise a woman who has given birth and the like, it is her duty to seek every remedy with all her strength in order to become pure for her husband one hour sooner. Included in this is that she should not delay her ritual immersion at its proper time even by a single day, for she does not know what a day of transgression may bring, God forbid. Now, when a man knows the number of days his wife will be in her niddah state, he is not as likely to have such improper thoughts, since he diverts his mind from her; but when he thinks her time to become pure has arrived and she has not yet become pure, that is the dangerous time, for every day he thinks, “Now she has immersed.” Therefore good counsel is that she should discuss it with her husband and tell him when she begins counting the clean days, through some sign in her clothing that they arrange between themselves, and if her count is interrupted, she should tell him again. And if, after all this effort and trouble, no remedy is found, it is her duty to permit her husband to marry another in addition to her, to save him from sin. And even though jealousy is as harsh as the grave, and a rival wife beside her [is hard to bear], the reward is according to the pain — how good is her portion and how pleasant is her lot.
